method: Mechanical checks plus separate quoted editorial reports. Neither establishes actual audio duration or a complete independent episode/book viewing.

editorial_validation.manual_final_edits: Book collection chain, opening artifact and CTA placement recorded separately where applicable.
editorial_validation.method: Three editorial passes, source-bounded fact checks, exact local corrections, editor examination of material findings and changed joins, mechanical and limited reference comparison. Not new full episode viewing or audio measurement.
editorial_validation.scope: Frank Herbert's six original Dune novels. Main evidence: Dune and Dune Messiah; later novels cover Leto II's leverage, Ixian navigation and concealment, Tleilaxu spice production and the changed conditions of travel. Book continuity; no expanded prequels/sequels or film-specific Navigator physiology.
editorial_validation.duration_gate: Measure generated voice >= 120 minutes before publication.

editorial_validation.final_formatting: Trailing line spaces removed after local corrections; no wording changed.

review_findings_before_final_local_edits.quote: That last part is why the cargo matters alongside the named passengers. The Duke's family can't run Arrakis through their presence alone. His soldiers need the means to operate, and his administrators need a working organization around them.  What we do know is that the Atreides arrive as a governing and military presence. Interstellar transport has made that transfer of organized activity possible.
review_findings_before_final_local_edits.reason: H18 identifies 'the same point restated with the wording shuffled.' The second paragraph already explains the transfer of a functioning government, and the intervening paragraphs establish the carriage of vessels and loads. This paragraph adds no distinct mechanism.

review_findings_before_final_local_edits.quote: The Guild has organized its navigational capacity on a different scale. Hawat belongs to the Atreides household, while the Guild supplies transport across the imperial order. Its monopoly means that rival Houses depend on the same institution for interstellar movement. A House can retain its own Mentat without gaining an independent equivalent of Guild navigation. The comparison helps explain why impressive human resources within a House don't make that House self-sufficient. Leto's household has Hawat, Jessica, and highly trained military leaders, yet its relocation still requires the carrier.
review_findings_before_final_local_edits.reason: The useful Mentat/Navigator distinction is followed by another extended relocation-and-monopoly explanation. H18 requires a re-mention to add a consequence or comparison; the comparison can be retained without repeating the prior chapters' full conclusion.
review_findings_before_final_local_edits.replacement: A House can retain its own Mentat without gaining an independent equivalent of Guild navigation. Hawat's analysis helps Leto govern and prepare, but it doesn't supply the foresight needed to guide a heighliner.

review_findings_before_final_local_edits.quote: Shields belong to the same description, although their practical role differs from that of atomics. Throughout Dune, shields shape how people defend themselves and how fighters approach an opponent. A household allowed to take them into exile retains familiar protective equipment. Herbert doesn't take us through a renegade family's departure, so the useful detail is the permission itself. The arrangement recognizes that a noble family consists of people who still need protection after losing their place in imperial politics. Survival continues to require material means once the political decision to leave has been made.
review_findings_before_final_local_edits.reason: This expands the previous paragraph's already explicit point that exiles retain defensive resources, then substitutes a methodological caveat and a general statement about survival for development of the sanctuary mechanism. H18's 're-stating it with nothing new attached' applies.

review_findings_before_final_local_edits.quote: Jessica's conservatory gives another measure of the differences inside the residence. Its plants require water on a planet where conserving moisture shapes everyday conduct. For Jessica, the room is a private place of greenery and a reminder of conditions she has left behind. Its existence also makes the household's privilege tangible. Leto can change the distribution of water at his door, yet he and his family still inhabit a residence that sustains such a room. The dinner takes place within that uneven world. A discussion of water can't remain an abstract exchange about sensible policy when the hosts and guests occupy such different positions from the people outside.
review_findings_before_final_local_edits.reason: The preceding water-merchant and towel paragraphs already establish the dinner's material inequalities. This additional location detour postpones the assigned banker's fear of Kynes without developing the banker's role or relationships. This is a local focus problem, not an objection to the analysis of privilege itself.

review_findings_before_final_local_edits.quote: For the banker, this makes the dinner a more complicated setting than a meeting between a financial official and his new provincial ruler. Kynes and Tuek have their own standing, and the banker must reckon with people beyond the Atreides household. His fear of Kynes is particularly striking beside the Guild name he carries. In this room, institutional prestige doesn't spare him from personal apprehension. An interpretation worth considering is that he recognizes local consequences which the newcomers haven't yet learned to anticipate. Jessica's attention stays on the reaction itself, because it helps her identify where caution already exists among people familiar with Arrakis.
review_findings_before_final_local_edits.reason: H18 applies: the preceding Kynes and Tuek paragraphs have already delivered the fear, alignment and contrast between formal rank and local standing. The closing paragraph returns to the same attributes again. This middle restatement is the least useful occurrence, and its proposed 'local consequences' remain unspecified.

review_findings_before_final_local_edits.quote: The Guild's dealings with the Fremen give it access to people largely hidden from imperial authorities, but they don't tell us how fully it understands them. The bargain secures spice and protects concealment; it doesn't give the Guild control over what Fremen communities may later do. Their eventual challenge to the rulers of Arrakis shows the limits of that arrangement, without establishing exactly what the Guild knew beforehand.
review_findings_before_final_local_edits.reason: The following paragraph immediately repeats that access does not establish understanding. H18's document-scale echo is compounded here by an evidence-limit explanation already made earlier in this chapter. Deleting this occurrence preserves the important uncertainty in the closing paragraph.

review_findings_before_final_local_edits.quote: Dune Messiah also gives us a glimpse of how uncomfortable this continuing arrangement is for the Guild. Edric participates in a conspiracy against Paul alongside people whose interests differ from his own. The details of their undertaking belong to that gathering, but his participation already tells us something about the imperial settlement. The Guild hasn't disappeared, and compliance hasn't made every Guild interest identical to Paul's. A Navigator can come into contact with the new imperial order while seeking a way to change the circumstances under which his organization must exist.
review_findings_before_final_local_edits.reason: Chapter 17 already introduces Edric's meeting and political role, and Chapter 19 opens with the full gathering. H18 requires re-mentions to develop the subject; this third introduction mainly announces material immediately ahead. The following paragraph independently preserves the useful cooperation-versus-loyalty conclusion.

review_findings_before_final_local_edits.quote: The no-ship on Gammu in Heretics of Dune gives the distinction a concrete setting. The ancient vessel hidden there becomes a refuge for people whose survival depends on escaping their pursuers. Its concealment and its capacity for travel both matter to their situation.
review_findings_before_final_local_edits.reason: This conflates the ancient Harkonnen no-globe used as a refuge on Gammu with a no-ship. The concealed refuge does not establish the claimed capacity for interstellar travel. That device distinction is especially important in a chapter expressly assigned to separate concealment from navigation.

review_findings_before_final_local_edits.quote: The destruction of Rakis gives this wider setting a concrete loss. The Honored Matres destroy the planet that once supplied the spice around which imperial transport was organized. The attack is devastating, and it destroys the familiar home of the sandworms. Yet the later story continues across other worlds. Ships still carry people, the Bene Gesserit continue their work, and the struggle with the Honored Matres continues. The old planet's destruction doesn't bring all human movement to an end.
review_findings_before_final_local_edits.reason: Chapter 25 has just narrated Rakis's destruction and the survival of other production possibilities. H18 requires the returning fact to carry its new consequence rather than replay the event. Here the useful new point is continued movement.
review_findings_before_final_local_edits.replacement: Even the destruction of Rakis doesn't end all human movement. The later struggle continues across worlds, showing how far travel has moved beyond dependence on the old planetary source.

review_findings_before_final_local_edits.quote: Before that destruction, a sandworm is removed from Rakis and taken to Chapterhouse. The Bene Gesserit undertake the transformation of their own world to establish the worm cycle there. That effort shows how much spice still matters after the Guild's exclusive position has weakened. The Sisterhood uses melange for purposes that navigation machines don't replace, including the practices of its Reverend Mothers. Moving a worm and changing a planet are demanding responses to the loss of Rakis. A substitute for a Navigator leaves those other needs in place.
review_findings_before_final_local_edits.reason: The rescued worm, Chapterhouse transformation and continued non-navigation demand all have a developed home in Chapter 25. H18's 'same point restated with the wording shuffled' applies. The next paragraph already supplies the necessary bridge through Chapterhouse's combination of independence and vulnerability.
